tldr: We propose a framework that adapts a simulation-trained multi-finger hand policy by having a human directly assist only the failing fingers to correct contact forces and trajectories, distilling them into a force-conditioned policy. It dramatically improves object flipping success rate from 14% to 86% and screwdriver rotation progress from 26% to 95%.
hero_caption: Overview of ReDex. When a simulation-trained base policy encounters contact failures on real hardware, a human physically repairs only the problematic fingers under compliant control while preserving the coordinated motion of the remaining fingers. Training targets are reconstructed from the resulting contact forces and trajectories to train a force-conditioned policy.
overview:
Combining reinforcement learning with physics simulation has enabled efficient learning of coordinated motions for advanced dexterous manipulation using multi-finger hands. However, the "Sim-to-Real gap" remains a major obstacle, as policies often fail on real hardware due to contact timing errors and minute contact force inaccuracies. Accurately reproducing friction and contact dynamics in a simulator is difficult, and repeatedly tuning domain randomization and reward functions incurs massive costs.

To address this, the authors observed that even when a policy fails on real hardware, the core multi-finger coordination backbone of the base policy remains intact, and contact failures are often confined to only a subset of fingers. Rather than reteaching everything from scratch, they propose "ReDex," an approach where a human gently guides only the problematic fingers on the fly under finger-level compliant intervention while letting the base policy continue driving the remaining fingers.

Specifically, joint stiffness (P-gain) is lowered only for the fingers being corrected so that a human can guide them, while contact forces are recorded using fingertip tactile sensors. Afterward, force-informed target joint positions are reconstructed offline from the corrected motions and contact forces, and behavior cloning is used to train a standalone policy with tactile feedback.

In experiments on a real 5-finger robot hand performing Object Flipping and Screwdriver Rotation, adding just a few minutes of human corrections per object substantially boosted base policy performance.
contributions: Developed a finger-level compliant intervention interface allowing a human to selectively correct failing fingers while maintaining automated control over the remaining fingers.
Established a relabeling method using a virtual spring model to reconstruct dense, force-informed target joint positions from corrected finger trajectories and fingertip tactile sensor measurements.

Demonstrated that a force-responsive real-world policy can be acquired with only a few minutes of correction per object, without tactile modeling in simulation or cumbersome full-hand teleoperation on real hardware.

sections.heading: Why is Sim-to-Real for dexterous hands hard, and how can we solve it?
sections.summary: Training multi-finger hands in simulation is powerful, but policies often fail to transfer to the real world due to discrepancies in contact timing and force regulation. ReDex achieves real-world adaptation with minimal human effort by leaving most coordination to the base policy while physically correcting only the failing fingers and incorporating force feedback.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-finger hands has advanced rapidly through massively parallel reinforcement learning in simulation. However, accurately modeling object contact dynamics in real environments is extremely challenging. When fingers make contact at unintended locations, contact too early, or apply too much or too little force, sim-to-real transfer breaks down.

Physical human correction (kinesthetic teaching or teleoperation) is a promising way to fix failures directly in real environments, but applying it to multi-finger hands has been notoriously difficult. It is hard for a human to manipulate multiple fingers simultaneously to maintain a stable grasp, glove-based teleoperation struggles to convey optimal contact forces, and collecting full-hand demonstrations from scratch imposes a massive burden.

The core insight here is that sim-to-real failures are often local. The base policy retains the multi-finger coordination patterns needed to progress through the task, and only the contact positions or force regulation of one or two fingers are broken. ReDex therefore allows a human operator to physically correct only the failed fingers under compliant control during real rollouts, while keeping the base policy running on the remaining fingers. Furthermore, it reconstructs training data by combining fingertip forces from tactile sensors and distills them into a force-conditioned policy.

sections.heading: At the intersection of RL, human intervention, and tactile learning
sections.summary: This work unifies three research lines: RL for dexterous manipulation, learning from human corrections, and tactile/contact feedback. It overcomes the heavy operational burden of traditional arm intervention techniques and full-hand teleoperation by focusing on localized, finger-level intervention.
sections.details:
### Dexterous Manipulation via Reinforcement Learning
Because direct real-world training or demonstration collection is prohibitively expensive, mainstream approaches rely on parallel simulation training, privileged information, and domain randomization (such as RMA). However, no matter how much randomization is applied, bridging the gap for real-world friction and actuator discrepancies remains difficult. ReDex chooses to preserve and leverage the multi-finger coordination patterns acquired in simulation.

### Learning from Human Correction
Interactive imitation learning frameworks like DAgger, TRANSIC, and CR-DAgger allow humans to provide corrections during robot execution. However, these primarily target manipulator arms. When extended to multi-finger hands, methods such as DexHiL and HandITL require retargeting human hand motions to correct all fingers, imposing a heavy burden on the operator. Conversely, DexScrew lets a human control only the wrist while retaining finger coordination, but it cannot fix individual finger contacts. ReDex achieves both coordination retention and local correction by intervening selectively on failing fingers.

### Learning Contact Feedback
Force feedback is crucial for contact-rich tasks. Methods like DexForce utilize contact forces during kinesthetic teaching, while others model tactile sensors inside simulators. However, the latter requires precise per-sensor calibration, and tactile modeling itself is extraordinarily difficult. ReDex takes a post-training approach, introducing force feedback on the real robot after base policy training, thereby acquiring a force-conditioned policy without incorporating a tactile model into the simulator.

sections.heading: ReDex algorithm and system architecture
sections.summary: ReDex consists of three steps: training a proprioception-only base policy in simulation, collecting finger-level compliant corrections on real hardware, and reconstructing force-informed action targets via a virtual spring model to distill the policy with behavior cloning.
sections.details:
### III-A Sim-to-Real Base Policy Training
First, a base policy for each task is trained in Isaac Sim following the Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) paradigm. After training a PPO teacher policy with privileged information, an adaptation module is trained to estimate latent variables from the history of past joint positions and action targets. When deployed to the real hardware, it takes only proprioception as input and outputs target joint positions $a_t^{\mathrm{RL}}$ for all fingers at 20 Hz.

### III-B Finger-Level Compliant Correction
During real-world execution of the base policy, the operator selects a subset of fingers $\mathcal{I}_t$ to correct using keyboard input, establishing a binary mask $m_t$. For joints of the selected fingers, proportional gains (P-gains) and torque limits are lowered, allowing the human to move them via external force (compliant control). Meanwhile, unselected fingers continue to track base policy commands at nominal gains. Corrected fingers are assigned targets $a_t^h$ that follow the human-guided positions, overriding the base policy targets to prevent conflict. Because the base policy receives the corrected finger joint states in its observation history, the remaining fingers naturally adapt to the modified hand state and continue the task.

### III-C Force-Informed Action Target Reconstruction
Kinesthetic teaching by a human provides joint angles $q_t$ (geometric kinematics), but it does not directly capture the contact forces the robot should exert. To address this, ReDex uses contact forces $\mathbf{f}_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ measured by magnetic tactile sensors on the corrected fingertips. Using the transpose of the fingertip translational Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{i,t}$, contact forces are converted into joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}^f_t$, and joint offsets $\Delta a_t^f = \mathbf{K}_f^{-1} \boldsymbol{\tau}_t^f$ are computed via a virtual spring model with a virtual joint stiffness matrix $\mathbf{K}_f$. Adding these to the base joint positions $q_t$ yields force-informed targets $a_t^f$. Finally, the base policy targets $a_t^{\mathrm{RL}}$ and force targets $a_t^f$ are composed according to mask $m_t$, and transitions are smoothed using minimum-jerk interpolation to create training labels $a_t^\star$.

### III-D Force-Conditioned Policy Learning
From the reconstructed trajectory data, a Behavior Cloning (BC) policy $\pi_\theta$ with Action Chunking is trained. Taking a 5-step history of joint positions and resultant fingertip forces as input, it predicts all-finger target joint positions for the next 16 steps at once. During inference at 20 Hz, the first 12 steps are executed before predicting the next chunk. This yields an autonomous policy capable of adapting to real-world force feedback.

sections.heading: Real-robot experimental setup and evaluation tasks
sections.summary: Using a 12-DoF 5-finger robot hand, the method was evaluated on two challenging tasks across five objects: Object Flipping and Screwdriver Rotation. Task success rate, rotation progress, and required human intervention time were measured in comparison to the base policy alone and residual learning baselines.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
A RobotEra XHAND1 12-DoF 5-finger hand was used for the experiments. Each fingertip is equipped with a 3-axis magnetic tactile array having 120 taxels; resultant forces are computed and transformed into the hand base frame.

The target tasks and evaluation metrics are as follows:
- **Object Flipping**: Evaluated on a cuboid (15 × 7 × 3 cm) and a smartphone (13.15 × 6.42 × 0.74 cm). The hand must reorient the object by 90 degrees while switching contact points in-hand and establish a stable grasp for success.
- **Screwdriver Rotation**: Evaluated on three screwdrivers: standard (2.6 cm diameter), slim (1.8 cm), and thick (3.5 cm). To evaluate finger gating (sequentially repositioning fingers to turn the tool), progress toward a full 360-degree rotation is measured (quantized into percentages in 90-degree increments).

In the primary evaluation, 25 autonomous trials were conducted for each method and object. BC policies were trained on 30 successful corrected rollouts per object for flipping, and 10 rollouts for screwdriver rotation.

Comparisons were made against simulation-only "RMA", as well as prior residual learning baselines trained on intervention data: "Gated Correction" and "Continuous Correction". Both residual baselines were trained using the same dataset and force-informed targets as ReDex.

sections.heading: Dramatic real-world performance gains and ablation analysis
sections.summary: ReDex boosted Object Flipping success rate from 14% to 86% and Screwdriver Rotation progress from 26.0% to 95.3%. It significantly outperformed residual baselines, demonstrating that force adaptation can be achieved with only a few minutes of finger intervention per object.
sections.details:
### Real-World Task Performance
On cuboid flipping and standard screwdriver rotation—which closely match simulation geometry—the base policy (RMA) achieved only a 16% (4/25) success rate on cuboid flipping and 26% rotation progress on the screwdriver. Mistimed finger releases and insufficient contact forces caused the screwdriver to drop. In contrast, ReDex improved these to 80% (20/25) on cuboid flipping and 95% on standard screwdriver rotation. It also substantially outperformed Gated Correction (12% flipping, 42% rotation) and Continuous Correction (4% flipping, 36% rotation). Residual approaches struggled with gating accuracy and residual scaling under limited intervention data, frequently degrading the base policy's intact behaviors.

### Adaptation to Object Variants
Without retraining the simulation base policy, ReDex adapted to novel object shapes and sizes with just minutes of real-world corrections. Slim screwdriver rotation progress jumped from 33% to 99%, thick screwdriver progress rose from 19% to 92%, and thin smartphone flipping success surged from 12% to 92%. The broad coordination backbone of the base policy coupled smoothly with human local corrections tailored to the real environment.

### Ablation Study and Tactile Representations
Component analysis on the cuboid flipping task (10 trials each) showed that while kinesthetic teaching alone achieved 4/10, adding tactile observations reached 6/10, force target reconstruction reached 7/10, and smoothing reached 6/10. The full ReDex method combining all components achieved the highest performance at 9/10. Without force targets, the thumb released prematurely and dropped the object; without smoothing, abrupt boundary transitions destabilized grasps. Regarding tactile representations, using resultant fingertip force vectors yielded higher success rates than raw taxel arrays, being less prone to sensor noise.

### Human Effort Reduction
For cuboid flipping, full kinesthetic teaching of all joints required 13.2 minutes of human intervention, whereas ReDex required only 2.4 minutes on the thumb alone—an 82% reduction in intervention time. Human intervention accounted for only 24.0% of total rollout time, while the base policy autonomously operated the fingers for the remaining 76%.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions
sections.summary: ReDex provides a highly practical framework for dexterous sim-to-real transfer: let a human fix only the failing fingers, incorporate tactile feedback, and distill the behavior. Extending to whole-body manipulation and addressing sensor drift remain key future challenges.
sections.details:
ReDex leverages the multi-finger coordination backbone learned in simulation while efficiently repairing local contact failures on real hardware through finger-level compliant interaction. Its major breakthrough is enabling the learning of an autonomous force-feedback policy from just minutes of teaching, without building complex tactile simulation models.

The authors highlight several avenues for future work: evaluating across diverse tactile sensor types, extending the framework to whole-body manipulation including the wrist and arm, and preserving the broad generalization capabilities of simulation training after real-world distillation.

takeaways: Sim-to-real failures in multi-finger hands are often localized; intervening only on problematic fingers while letting the base policy handle healthy fingers is highly effective.
Applying offline force adjustments via fingertip tactile sensors and a virtual spring model to human geometric demonstrations generates action targets that account for contact forces.
Force-conditioned behavior cloning from a small set of real-world corrections yields robust autonomous policies without complex tactile simulation or residual policy gain tuning.
limitations: Excessive or poorly timed human interventions can disrupt coordination phase with other fingers, driving states out of the base policy's training distribution and causing subsequent execution to fail.
Distilling from a small number of real-world trajectories may compromise some of the broad domain robustness and generalization gained during simulation training.
Magnetic tactile sensors suffer from sensor drift, making it difficult to distinguish post-tare baseline drift from true changes in contact force.
